Regression analyses investigated associations between baseline characteristics of patients and physiotherapists and alliance. Results: Table 1 and 2 present characteristics of patients and therapists. Table 3 presents therapeutic alliance ratings for each of the 3 sub‐scales as well as overall scores. At week 4, patients rated the overall alliance, as well as all sub‐scales, significantly higher than therapists. At 26 weeks, patients rated the task sub‐scale significantly higher than therapists. Over time, patient ratings for total alliance and goal sub‐scale decreased, while physiotherapist ratings for total alliance and bond sub‐scale increased. Table 4 displays the patient and therapist characteristics that were significantly associated with total alliance scores. For patients, living with others, consulting with a therapist with previous training in behaviour change, and having high self‐efficacy was associated with greater alliance ratings. Therapists were more likely to perceive a stronger alliance if they were less experienced delivering care remotely and when treating patients who were younger, employed, and with higher self‐efficacy. Conclusions: Patients rated the therapeutic alliance significantly higher than therapists early in treatment, with scores generally converging by the end of treatment. A number o individual characteristics were associated with alliance scores. Findings suggest that clinicians should not assume that their perceptions of the alliance reflect those of their patients. Clinicians may need to utilise more person‐centred practice principles to strengthen the alliance with some sub‐groups of patients, such as those with low self‐efficacy, who are less likely to perceive a strong alliance over the telephone.
